report:
## Conclusion: The claim is well-supported, though the strength of evidence is "probable" rather than definitive.

**Key evidence:**

The largest and most rigorous trial is the NEJM randomized trial (Tuuli et al.), which found chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep resulted in a **significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection** after cesarean delivery compared with iodine-alcohol (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048). A separate large single-center RCT similarly found significantly lower SSI rates with chlorhexidine-alcohol vs. povidone-iodine-alcohol (6.95% vs. 14.28%, P=0.005) (https://www.ijrcog.org/index.php/ijrcog/article/view/6461).

However, not all trials agree — the CAPICA trial found povidone-iodine remained acceptable and did not show a clear chlorhexidine advantage (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/), and a pilot RCT found a favorable trend for chlorhexidine that didn't reach statistical significance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/).

Pooled evidence resolves this heterogeneity in chlorhexidine's favor. The Cochrane systematic review (updated through 2020) concluded that chlorhexidine gluconate is "probably slightly more effective" than povidone-iodine at reducing SSI after cesarean, while noting more high-quality research is still needed (https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section). A 2024 network meta-analysis also found alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being the most effective antiseptic for preventing SSI in cesarean sections, though credible intervals overlapped with other options.

**Bottom line:** Multiple RCTs and systematic reviews, including a Cochrane review, support a moderate SSI-reduction benefit from chlorhexidine-alcohol over iodine-based preparations, though individual trial results vary and effect sizes are modest — consistent with your view, with an appropriate caveat about ongoing uncertainty.
